target.title: fix(ollama): use CJK-aware char estimate for usage fallback
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Ollama's chat stream reports real usage via `prompt_eval_count`/`eval_count`
on the final response chunk. When those fields are missing or invalid (e.g. a
native stream that ends early), `extensions/ollama/src/stream.ts` falls back
to estimating tokens as `chars / 4` using plain UTF-16 `.length` on the
message content, tool-call JSON, and tool names.

That heuristic assumes ~4 chars/token, which holds for Latin/English text but
badly undercounts CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) text, which tokenizes at
roughly 1 char/token. For CJK-heavy conversations that hit this fallback path,
usage is undercounted by 2-4x.

This fallback usage feeds `assistantMessage.usage`, which is used both for
usage/context telemetry (`/context`, treemap, totals) and for
`calculateContextTokens` → `shouldCompact` proactive context-window
compaction decisions. Undercounting on CJK sessions means the agent believes
it has more context headroom than it actually does, delaying proactive
compaction until the provider itself errors on overflow.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core already has the correct weighting formula in `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts`
(`estimateStringChars`). Ollama's extension cannot import core internals, and
exposing that helper through the public plugin SDK would create a new stable
API commitment for a single consumer. This change mirrors the core weighting
locally in `extensions/ollama/src/cjk-char-estimate.ts` and applies it on the
production stream fallback path only.

This change:
- Weights message content, tool names, serialized tool fields, and completion
  text with the CJK-aware char estimate before the existing `chars / 4`
  rounding.
- Leaves provider-reported `prompt_eval_count` / `eval_count` authoritative
  when present.
- Proves the production caller path over real loopback HTTP (no fetch mock):
  `createOllamaStreamFn` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → NDJSON final chunk without
  eval counts → `done.message.usage`.

## User Impact

No change for ASCII/Latin content (the fallback estimate is unchanged for
that case). For CJK-heavy Ollama conversations that hit the native-usage
fallback path, usage/context accounting and proactive compaction triggering
are now accurate instead of undercounting by 2-4x. When Ollama does report
valid eval counts, those values remain authoritative.

## Evidence

- Changed: `extensions/ollama/src/stream.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/cjk-char-estimate.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts`,
  `extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts`
- Production caller path: `createOllamaStreamFn` → guarded fetch → NDJSON parse →
  fallback estimators → `buildAssistantMessage` → `done.message.usage`
- Compatibility: provider-reported eval counts still win over the fallback
- No public plugin-SDK export added

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior or issue addressed

When an Ollama-shaped NDJSON stream's final chunk omits `prompt_eval_count` /
`eval_count`, the production stream path writes CJK-aware fallback usage onto
`done.message.usage` (roughly 1 token per CJK char) instead of the old raw
UTF-16 `length / 4` undercount. Valid provider-reported eval counts still
override the fallback.

### Canonical reachability path

`createOllamaStreamFn` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → `/api/chat` NDJSON final chunk
without eval counts → `estimateOllamaPromptTokens` /
`estimateOllamaCompletionTokens` → `buildAssistantMessage` →
`done.message.usage`

### Shared helper / provider constraint check

Local `estimateStringChars` mirrors `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts` so the extension
stays inside the plugin boundary without growing the public SDK surface.
Provider-reported eval counts remain authoritative via `resolveUsageCount`.

### Real environment tested

Real HTTP transport: local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1` speaking Ollama
NDJSON `/api/chat`. The production `createOllamaStreamFn` path uses the real
`fetchWithSsrFGuard` (no SSRF mock) against that live socket. Final chunk
omits eval counts to force the fallback; sibling case keeps
`prompt_eval_count=77` / `eval_count=19` to prove provider counts stay
authoritative. Node v22.23.1.

### Exact steps or command run after this patch

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts \
  extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose
```

### Evidence after fix

```text
 ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts > createOllamaStreamFn thinking events > falls back to CJK-aware usage when the final chunk omits eval counts 1ms
 ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts > createOllamaStreamFn thinking events > keeps provider-reported eval counts authoritative over the CJK fallback 0ms
 ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/ollama/src/stream.test.ts > createOllamaStreamFn thinking events > matches the plain chars/4 heuristic for ASCII-only fallback usage 0ms
 ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts > createOllamaStreamFn CJK usage fallback (real HTTP) > estimates CJK-aware usage when a real Ollama-shaped stream omits eval counts 28ms
 ✓ |extension-providers| extensions/ollama/src/stream.usage-fallback.http.proof.test.ts > createOllamaStreamFn CJK usage fallback (real HTTP) > keeps provider-reported eval counts authoritative over the HTTP fallback 4ms

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  21 passed (21)
```

### Observed result after fix

Against a live loopback Ollama NDJSON server (real guarded fetch, no mock), a
CJK prompt/completion whose final chunk omits eval counts yields fallback
`usage.input` / `usage.output` that match `estimateStringChars(...)/4` and are
more than 2x the naive `length/4` undercount. When the final chunk includes
valid eval counts, those exact provider numbers are preserved on
`done.message.usage`.

### What was not tested

Live generation against a real Ollama daemon binary. The fallback trigger proven
here is the same production path that runs after NDJSON parse when eval counts
are absent or invalid; a daemon that always emits counts would not enter this
path without an intervening strip/proxy.

### Fix classification

bugfix — usage accounting / CJK undercount

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the local CJK mirror (no public SDK export),
real-HTTP caller-path proof, and CI unused-export cleanup.

target.title: fix(line): cap message action text length
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

LINE message actions carry a `text` field that LINE sends back as the user's message when the action is tapped. LINE caps that field at 300 characters, but OpenClaw's shared `messageAction()` helper only truncated the visible action label and let the emitted `text` payload pass through unchanged.

That creates an API-contract mismatch: OpenClaw can build a quick reply, template button, confirm action, carousel action, card-command action, or rich-menu action whose label is valid while its message-action `text` is still longer than LINE allows. In practice, the malformed action object is constructed before the payload reaches the LINE SDK send boundary.

The narrow pre-fix trigger was:

```ts
messageAction("Go", "x".repeat(301)).text.length === 301
```

The affected user-realistic path is:

```text
quick replies / template buttons / confirm actions / carousel actions / card commands / rich menus
  -> messageAction(label, text)
  -> LINE SDK payload
  -> LINE Messaging API
```

A long upstream command label, prompt-produced quick reply, card action, or template action can become user-visible LINE UI while still carrying over-limit message-action data. When LINE rejects that action payload, the user can lose the intended interactive reply/button instead of receiving a tappable action.

## Why This Change Was Made

The production change stays at the shared action-constructor boundary, but now uses a LINE message-action-specific grapheme cap instead of the UTF-16 action-data cap used by postback and datetime picker data:

```diff
 export function messageAction(label: string, text?: string): Action {
   return {
     type: "message",
     label: truncateLineActionLabel(label),
-    text: text ?? label,
+    text: truncateLineMessageText(text ?? label),
   };
 }
```

This keeps the fix centralized for all `messageAction()` callers while matching LINE's message-action text counting contract. It avoids the stricter UTF-16 behavior that would incorrectly shorten valid non-BMP emoji or composite grapheme text.

Unchanged sibling behavior: label truncation, URI actions, postback actions, datetime-picker actions, template layout, quick-reply routing, target normalization, send/reply behavior, and LINE client construction all stay as they were. Only message-action `text` is capped before the action object leaves the helper.

## User Impact

LINE users can receive quick replies, template buttons, confirm buttons, carousel actions, card-command actions, and rich-menu message actions even when an upstream prompt or command produces an overlong action text.

Instead of sending an action payload that exceeds LINE's contract, OpenClaw now truncates message action text on a grapheme boundary, matching LINE's message-action text contract without silently shortening valid emoji-heavy messages.

## Evidence

LINE's Messaging API reference documents message action `text` as the text sent as the user's message when the action is tapped and caps it at 300 characters. LINE's text-counting documentation distinguishes message-action `text` as grapheme-cluster-counted, so non-BMP emoji and composite graphemes must not be truncated by UTF-16 code-unit length.

References:

- https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#message-action
- https://developers.line.biz/en/docs/messaging-api/text-character-count/

After this change, the focused helper tests prove both the ASCII cap and grapheme boundary behavior:

```ts
messageAction("Go", "x".repeat(301)).text.length === 300
messageAction("Go", "\u{1f600}".repeat(300)).text === "\u{1f600}".repeat(300)
messageAction("Go", "e\u0301".repeat(301)).text === "e\u0301".repeat(300)
```

After-fix outbound-path proof was added at the LINE SDK boundary. The tests enter the same user-facing quick-reply send path and capture the payload passed to `MessagingApiClient.pushMessage()`:

```text
pushTextMessageWithQuickReplies("line:user:U123", "Pick one", ["x".repeat(301)], ...)
  -> createTextMessageWithQuickReplies()
  -> createQuickReplyItems()
  -> messageAction(label, label)
  -> MessagingApiClient.pushMessage({ messages: [{ quickReply: ... }] })
```

The captured quick-reply action text is now capped before it leaves OpenClaw's LINE send stack, including emoji-heavy inputs:

```ts
expect(quickReplyItem.action?.text).toHaveLength(300)
expect(graphemeLength(emojiQuickReply.action.text)).toBe(300)
```

Live LINE proof was also run from this PR branch against a test LINE Official Account and redacted test target:

```text

ASCII input action text: 301 UTF-16 code units
API-facing ASCII action text after fix: 300 UTF-16 code units
output ends with dangling high surrogate: false
```

target.title: fix(model-selection): preserve pinned override when the model catalog is degraded
target.body:
Related: #97517

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where switching an active session to a model served by a slow-to-start runtime (e.g. `/model codex/gpt-5.5` behind a local app-server/proxy) would, on the first turn or two, show a misleading rejection and silently unpin the user's chosen model:

```
Model override codex/gpt-5.5 is not allowed for this agent; reverted to <fallback>.
Add codex/gpt-5.5 to agents.defaults.models or pick an allowed model with /model list.
```

The model **is** allowed — it is inherited from `agents.defaults.models`. The real trigger is a transient cold-start/discovery failure: for that one turn the live model catalog fails to load, so the pinned model looks disallowed. Worse, the reset was **persisted**, permanently unpinning the model, and the notice told the user to "add it to agents.defaults.models" — advice that is wrong and does not help. This is symptom #1 of #97517.

## Why This Change Was Made

The per-turn model catalog can load in a degraded state (discovery threw, or it fell back to a static/empty catalog). A degraded catalog cannot prove a pin is truly disallowed, yet the reset path treated a degraded `allowsKey() === false` identically to a genuine, authoritative rejection — destroying durable session state on a transient signal.

This change threads authoritative-vs-degraded provenance through `ModelCatalogSnapshot` (`authoritative?: boolean`; only degraded loads set `false`). When a pin is rejected **only** because the catalog is degraded, the override is preserved: the turn still falls back to the primary model (unchanged behavior, via the existing `allowsKey` gate), and a non-destructive "temporarily unavailable" notice is shown instead of the destructive "not allowed; add to config" message. The pin is re-evaluated once discovery recovers.

Genuine disallow (authoritative catalog proves the model is gone) and stale overrides (a catalog-independent config fact) keep today's destructive reset — both are reliable signals, so their behavior is unchanged.

Scope: this addresses symptom #1 (the false "not allowed; reverted" misreport). Symptom #2 in the issue (`/status` runtime label lagging the live-switched harness) is a separate persisted-snapshot path and is not touched here.

## User Impact

- A pinned model served by a slow-starting runtime is no longer silently unpinned during its cold-start window. Once the runtime finishes its first handshake, the pin is simply used.
- During the transient window the user sees an accurate, non-alarming notice ("temporarily unavailable; using <primary> for this turn; your pinned model is unchanged") instead of a misleading allow-list rejection with unhelpful config advice.
- No change for genuinely disallowed or stale overrides — those still reset as before.

## Evidence

**Unit tests** (`src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.test.ts`) — new `degraded-catalog override preservation` block, all green, covering the three branches that differ only by catalog provenance:
- degraded catalog + pin the catalog cannot vouch for → **preserved**, reason `temporarily-unavailable`, pin untouched, turn falls back to primary;
- authoritative catalog proving the pin is gone → **destructive reset**, reason `disallowed` (unchanged);
- authoritative catalog containing the pin → no reset, pin used.

**Live, real code + real key** (no mocks):
- `loadModelCatalogSnapshot({ readOnly: true })` → real static-fallback path returns `authoritative: false` (degraded) — verified.
- Real OpenAI key → real discovery → `authoritative !== false` with real `openai` catalog entries present — verified against the live provider (this is the exact per-turn catalog-load path the gateway runs). Discovery-failure with no credentials likewise returns `authoritative: false`, confirming degraded marking end-to-end.

The transient degraded **window itself** cannot be triggered on demand through a live message (it depends on a runtime cold-start race), so that branch is covered by the unit tests plus the verified real-code provenance marking rather than a live message round-trip.

**Static checks:** `tsgo` typecheck clean, `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean, autoreview (uncommitted diff) clean — no accepted/actionable findings.

target.title: fix(openrouter): add model-aware tool schema normalization for proxied providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Models routed through OpenRouter that reject `anyOf`/`oneOf` in tool parameter schemas (Moonshot/Kimi K3, DeepSeek, Google/Gemini) receive raw unsanitized schemas and return HTTP 400 — "provider rejected the request schema or tool payload."

The ClawRouter extension already handles this via `resolveToolFamily()` model-prefix routing, but the OpenRouter extension registers no `normalizeToolSchemas` or `inspectToolSchemas` hooks. Tool schemas pass through verbatim regardless of the downstream provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

Kimi K3 (`moonshotai/kimi-k3`) via OpenRouter fails on tool calls that include `anyOf`/`oneOf` unions in parameter schemas — common in MCP-sourced tools and TypeBox-defined tools. The model handles basic chat completions fine, but 400s on tool payloads.

The root cause: `extensions/openrouter/index.ts` has no tool schema normalization, unlike `extensions/clawrouter/index.ts` which routes models to the correct compat family (`deepseek`, `gemini`, `openai`) based on model ID prefix.

## User Impact

Users running Moonshot/Kimi, DeepSeek, or Google models through OpenRouter will no longer get `400 Provider returned error` on tool calls. The fix applies the same schema normalization that direct provider plugins and ClawRouter already use.

## Evidence

- Observed in production: `moonshotai/kimi-k3` via OpenRouter returns 200 for basic chat but 400 when tools with `anyOf`/`oneOf` schemas are included
- `providerRuntimeFailureKind: "schema"` in gateway diagnostic logs
- ClawRouter already implements the identical pattern at `extensions/clawrouter/index.ts:105-117`
- DeepSeek direct provider uses `buildProviderToolCompatFamilyHooks("deepseek")` at `extensions/deepseek/index.ts:55`

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector. When the sidecar exceeds the cap during writes, it is archived and a fresh file is started so SQLite persistence continues.

## Changes

1. **Bounded reads**: `loadCronQuarantineFile` uses the shared `readRegularFile` helper with an 8 MiB cap instead of unbounded `fs.promises.readFile`.
2. **Bounded writes**: `saveCronQuarantineFile` checks the serialized payload size before writing. If it exceeds 8 MiB, the existing file is archived and a fresh file with only the new entries is created. If a single entry alone exceeds the cap, writes fail with a clear error.
3. **Archive retention**: Archived sidecar files use a fixed name (`*.archive.json`), so repeated overflows overwrite the previous archive instead of creating an unbounded collection of uniquely named files that can exhaust disk.
4. **Tests**: Regression coverage for bounded reads, oversized write rejection, archive creation and fresh-start recovery, and single-archive retention after repeated overflows.

## User Impact

A corrupted or oversized quarantine sidecar is rejected before OOM. When the sidecar grows past 8 MiB during cron operations, the overflow is archived and a fresh sidecar is started, keeping cron persistence alive. Archives do not accumulate.

## Evidence

### Real test output: all 6 PR-specific tests pass

The actual `src/cron/store.test.ts` test suite was run against the PR's code. All 6 quarantine-related tests pass, demonstrating bounded reads, write rejection, archive rotation, and single-archive retention. The sole test failure is a SQLite-dependent pre-existing test (`lets doctor import legacy top-level array jobs into SQLite and archive the source`) that cannot run locally due to Node 24.13.1's embedded SQLite 3.51.2 (the code requires SQLite 3.51.3+ for WAL safety).

```
 ✓ |cron| fails closed instead of overwriting unrecognized quarantine files
 ✓ |cron| rejects oversized quarantine files to prevent OOM
 ✓ |cron| rejects writing a quarantine sidecar that would exceed the byte cap
 ✓ |cron| archives an existing quarantine sidecar and starts fresh when the cap is exceeded
 ✓ |cron| keeps only one archive after repeated overflows
 ✓ |cron| does not rewrite quarantine files when every entry is already present

 Tests:  1 failed (SQLite-dependent pre-existing test), 6 passed, 44 skipped
```

The 6 passing tests directly exercise the PR's bounded read (`readRegularFile` with 8 MiB cap), bounded write (payload size check before persistence), archive rotation (oversized sidecar archived, fresh file started), and single-archive retention (`*.archive.json` overwritten on repeated overflow).

### Subsystem warning output (via rawConsole capture)

When `loadCronQuarantineFile` encounters an oversized file, the subsystem logger emits a warn-level message through the `cron/store` subsystem:

```
[WARN] [cron/store] Quarantine file at .../cron-quarantine.json exceeds the 8388608-byte limit
```

The quarantine file is rejected and the cron load path continues without loading the corrupted state.

Fixes an issue where the `plugin-npm-release` workflow could remain stuck in any of its six `git fetch` steps or the `npm publish` step until the job timeout when the Git transport or npm registry stalls. This blocks plugin npm releases and wastes runner time.

## Why This Change Was Made

All six `git fetch` commands and the `npm publish` command now run through the repository's bounded process pattern: a 120-second deadline, followed by a 10-second termination grace period. This matches the pattern already applied to Mantis Crabbox workflows in #108940 (commit 16c2bbb). All release logic, merge-base checks, and non-network operations are unchanged.

The six fetch locations: extended-stable branch fetch (L134), main+release fetch (L141), alpha branch fetch (L162), source SHA fetch (L622), main fetch (L1102), and target SHA fetch (L1140). The npm publish (L1329) also receives the same timeout.

## User Impact

Maintainers get prompt, actionable failures instead of losing a plugin release runner for the full job timeout.

## Evidence

- Controlled runtime proof extracted each production workflow step, scaled the production deadline to one second, and injected a stalled transport for each network operation. Every step returned 124 in about 1.03 seconds and did not reach the five-second outer watchdog. The identical pattern was proven in #108940 and accepted in #109174.

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check` passed for the changed file; `git diff --check` passed.

- The complete test suite was also attempted: all tests passed, while unrelated environment-dependent cases were skipped. The affected regression is green.

target.title: fix: readability extraction handles raw-text pseudo tags
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users fetching readable HTML pages could lose Readability extraction when the page embeds large client-side templates or style/script text containing strings such as repeated `<div>` tags.

The user-realistic path is:

```text
web_fetch -> runWebFetch(text/html) -> extractReadableContent -> web-readability extractor -> sanitizeHtml -> exceedsEstimatedHtmlNestingDepth -> Readability result or fallback
```

Before this fix, the nesting preflight scanned raw HTML text inside elements such as `<script>` and could count pseudo tags in JavaScript/CSS/template text as real DOM nesting. On an otherwise readable article, that made the extractor return `null`, so `web_fetch` could fall back to provider/basic HTML extraction instead of returning the higher-quality Readability result.

## Why This Change Was Made

The web-readability nesting preflight now treats the targeted raw-text/RCDATA and legacy raw-text-like element contents as text while preserving the existing depth guard for real markup outside those elements. It still counts the element itself and still enforces the maximum nesting depth for the rest of the document.

The start-tag scan is quote-aware but remains bounded, so a quoted attribute value like `data-close="</script>"` cannot make the preflight resume scanning inside a raw-text start tag, and malformed apparent tags cannot trigger an unbounded scan. This PR does not change fetch behavior, provider fallback behavior, SSRF/network policy, the 1 MB readability limit, or the general Readability parser.

## User Impact

`web_fetch` keeps readable article extraction quality on modern pages that include embedded JavaScript, CSS, or legacy fallback/template text containing HTML-like content. Pages that are genuinely too deeply nested still hit the same safety guard, and malformed fetched HTML remains bounded during the preflight.

## Evidence

User-realistic proof:

- Entry point checked: `web_fetch` on `text/html` content with the default readable extraction path.
- Before-fix runtime probe on upstream `main`: an otherwise readable article with `"<div>".repeat(3101)` inside `<script>` returned `{ "hasResult": false, "title": null, "textStart": null }`.
- After-fix runtime probe with the same pseudo-tag payload plus a quoted raw-text attribute boundary returned:

```json
{"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
```

Reviewer-feedback proof added after ClawSweeper review:

```text
noembed  {"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
noframes {"hasResult":true,"title":"Example Article","textStart":"Main content starts here wit"}
```

The second probe uses repeated apparent tags inside `<noembed>...</noembed>` and `<noframes>...</noframes>` content. A malformed apparent-tag flood probe with `"<a".repeat(50000)` completed and returned the expected fallback signal:

```json
{"result":null,"elapsedMs":11}
```

Focused validation:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.test.ts` - passed, 1 file / 7 tests.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.ts extensions/web-readability/web-content-extractor.test.ts` - passed.
- `git diff --check` - passed.

Additional checks:

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions` still fails locally in untouched `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts` with existing errors around `BlockedIpv6Range` values `"benchmarking"`, `"orchid2"`, and a union callable at line 367. The earlier remote `check-prod-types` passed on this PR before the reviewer-feedback commits; remote CI is the source of truth for the updated head.
- Open PR/issue search for `web-readability readability nesting script style raw-text extractor` returned no matching open duplicate.
- HTML raw-text/RCDATA behavior was checked against the WHATWG HTML parsing model. `noscript` is intentionally not folded into this preflight set because it can contain meaningful fallback markup under scripting-disabled parsing behavior.
- This PR only changes extractor logic and colocated tests. It has no persistent data-model, migration, or upgrade compatibility change.

target.title: fix(ui): long chats retain generated image memory
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users viewing many managed outgoing images in a long-lived Control UI session would retain every fetched image Blob URL and failed lookup key for the browser process lifetime. That state grew with each unique image or miss, and Blob URLs were never revoked.

## Why This Change Was Made

The managed-image success and miss caches now retain at most 64 recently used entries. Successful entries use least-recently-used ordering and revoke the evicted Blob URL; miss entries use the same bounded retention while preserving the existing 5-second retry window. In-flight request deduplication and image rendering behavior remain unchanged.

This is independent of #108116: that PR bounds stalled fetch duration, while this PR bounds process-lifetime retained cache state.

## User Impact

Long-running Control UI chat sessions no longer accumulate managed generated-image cache state without limit. Recently viewed previews remain cached, and an evicted preview is fetched again if revisited.

## Evidence

Exact proof head: `2296e25844fd7045084f7fd09dd3669e4676a018`.

### Real Chromium Control UI proof

The committed E2E starts the real Vite Control UI in Playwright Chromium, supplies 64 managed outgoing images through the mocked Gateway, intercepts their real browser HTTP fetches, and wraps the browser's native `URL.createObjectURL` / `URL.revokeObjectURL` calls for diagnostics. It then:

1. revisits image 1 to make it most-recently-used;
2. loads image 65 and verifies image 2's Blob URL was revoked while image 1's was retained;
3. revisits evicted image 2 and verifies a second HTTP fetch plus a successfully decoded 160px preview.

Command:

```text
OPENCLAW_CAPTURE_UI_PROOF=1 OPENCLAW_BEHAVIOR_PROOF=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts --configLoader runner ui/src/e2e/chat-flow.e2e.test.ts -t "evicts and refetches managed image Blob URLs after the cache reaches capacity"
```

Redacted browser diagnostic:

```json
{"proof":"managed-image-cache","cacheCapacity":64,"createdBlobUrls":66,"evictedBlobIndex":1,"evictedImageFetches":2,"refetchedImageNaturalWidth":160,"retainedRecentBlobRevoked":false,"revokedBlobUrls":2}
```

Result: 1 passed, 52 skipped. The proof command also writes the inspected browser screenshot and JSON diagnostics to `.artifacts/control-ui-e2e/managed-image-cache/after-refetch.{png,json}`. The screenshot contains only the synthetic managed preview and the redacted counters above.

- Production regression head: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.ts` — 1 file, 94 tests passed.

target.title: refactor(state): move device identity into canonical SQLite state
target.body:
Related: #107227

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still treated `identity/device.json` as the authoritative device identity store while global runtime state had moved to SQLite. That left a second mutable state owner, made Node and Apple clients persist the same Ed25519 identity differently, and kept runtime behavior coupled to a legacy sidecar.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the stable device identity keypair into the existing typed `device_identities` table in the shared state database. Runtime code reads and writes SQLite only. `openclaw doctor --fix` owns the one-time, validated JSON import: it claims the unchanged source, verifies the canonical row, then removes the legacy file. Node and Swift share canonical PEM key material and the same device ID derivation.

The change is additive at the database layer: it reuses the already-shipped table and does not advance `user_version`. It does not change the device ID, signing payload, Gateway wire format, CLI JSON shape, pairing model, or legacy import document. Device auth tokens remain a separate migration because their gateway-scoped key requires a different additive table.

## User Impact

Existing valid identities keep the same device ID and keys, so upgrades do not require re-pairing. Legacy files fail closed until Doctor performs the explicit migration. Invalid or conflicting material is preserved for diagnosis; Doctor can repair an invalid canonical row, with a new identity and reapproval only when the original key material cannot be recovered.

This is a one-way database-first cutover. After Doctor retires the JSON source, downgrading to an older JSON-only binary can create a different identity. Aligned upgrades are therefore required across processes sharing the state directory.

## Evidence

- Full changed-surface gate passed on Node 24.18.0: TypeScript checks, lint, focused test shards, database-first guards, import-cycle checks, and SwiftLint. The remote Testbox sync timed out before running code, so the trusted-source fallback ran locally under the repository-supported Node and Xcode toolchains.
- Focused Node proof: 43 tests passed across device identity, Doctor migration, and node identity CLI suites.
- Focused Swift proof: 25 `DeviceIdentityStoreTests` passed, including Node PEM interoperability, timestamp reconciliation, auth ownership conflicts, profile isolation, strict legacy validation, schema gates, and WAL behavior.
- SwiftLint: 0 violations across macOS, helpers, shared, and iOS sources.
- Source-blind CLI behavior validation exercised valid legacy refusal, explicit Doctor import, exact identity preservation in a later process, and malformed-source preservation.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh automated review found and drove fixes for corrupt-row recovery, migration races, Doctor mutation authority, metadata-only key rotation, native auth ownership conflicts, and Swift timestamp equality. The final whole-branch autoreview scanner then stopped before model invocation on synthetic device-key/test-token material; two independent read-only final reviews covered migration/race/security and Swift–Node interoperability instead.

AI-assisted: yes. I understand and reviewed the resulting runtime, migration, cryptographic, and native-client behavior.

target.title: refactor(gateway): remove forward-referenced resolve in createTimeoutRace
target.body:
Closes #106645

## What Problem This Solves

Removes a brittle code smell in the gateway shutdown path. `createTimeoutRace` in `src/gateway/server-close.ts` scheduled its `setTimeout` before declaring the promise's `resolve`, relying on a `let resolve!` non-null assertion and a forward reference from the timer callback to a variable assigned further down. It worked only because the Promise executor happens to run synchronously, so the pattern was one refactor away from a latent "resolve is not a function" bug.

## Why This Change Was Made

The timer is now created inside the Promise executor, where `resolve` is already in scope, so the non-null assertion and the forward reference both go away. Behavior is identical: the promise still resolves with `onTimeout()` after `timeoutMs`, the timer is still `unref()`-ed so it does not keep the process alive, and `clear()` still cancels a pending timer. The redundant `clearTimeout` that the fired callback used to call on itself is dropped (a fired timer needs no cancellation).

## User Impact

None user-visible — this is an internal refactor of the shutdown/restart timeout helper. It removes a fragile pattern so future edits to the shutdown path are less likely to regress.

## Evidence

**Real gateway runs on this branch** (`openclaw gateway run --dev --port 18999` with an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, macOS, Node 22.22.2), exercising both `createTimeoutRace` outcomes:

1. Graceful SIGTERM shutdown with no connected clients — every timeout race resolves via `clear()`:

```
[gateway] ready
[gateway] signal SIGTERM received
[gateway] received SIGTERM; shutting down
[shutdown] started: gateway stopping
[shutdown] completed cleanly in 96ms
```
Port 18999 confirmed free after exit.

2. Graceful SIGTERM shutdown with a live WebSocket client held open — the websocket-close grace race actually fires its `onTimeout` path (`WEBSOCKET_CLOSE_GRACE_MS` = 1000ms) and shutdown continues normally:

```
ws client: connected
[gateway] signal SIGTERM received
[shutdown] started: gateway stopping
[shutdown] websocket server close exceeded 1000ms; forcing shutdown continuation with 1 tracked client(s)
[shutdown] completed in 1089ms with warnings: websocket-server
ws client: closed code=1006
```
Port 18999 confirmed free after exit; the client observed the server-initiated close.

**Automated coverage** — the existing shutdown suite drives every `createTimeoutRace` call site (grace/force websocket close, restart persistence waits, dispose timeouts):

```

 Test Files  2 passed (2)

```

`git diff --numstat`: `7  11  src/gateway/server-close.ts` (net -4 lines).

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `cd3cf83e4caeada7cba332ea0b89b4481df2e9d5` (rebased onto latest `upstream/main`).

### CLI transcript proof (exact head, redacted)

Actual `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` output at this exact HEAD (**09908298**). The `--dev` flag isolates state under `~/.openclaw-dev/`; stale plugin config warnings are redacted for brevity.

**Test 1 — Normal identity file (normal.md):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/normal-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...config warnings redacted...]
{
  "agentId": "test-agent",
  "identity": {
    "name": "CLI Proof Agent",
    "emoji": "🧪"
  },
  "workspace": "/tmp/...",
  "identityFile": "/tmp/.../normal-identity.md"
}
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 0 — identity file loaded and parsed correctly; identity values returned in JSON output.

**Test 2 — Oversized identity file (2,097,153 bytes = cap + 1):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/oversized-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...state migration output redacted...]
Identity file /tmp/oversized-identity.md exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 1 — oversized file rejected with the exact diagnostic `Identity file <path> exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes`. No identity configuration was written.

The oversized-file error message is identical to what the CLI prints to stderr before exiting with code 1. This confirms the full CLI code path (command handler → bounded loader → error reporting) works correctly at this exact HEAD (**09908298**) (**09908298**).

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 386ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

### Code overview

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` delegates to the same bounded loader and surfaces the size-limit error to the user.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` and `src/commands/agents.identity.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

target.title: feat(ui): Labs settings page for experimental feature toggles
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Experimental features (Code Mode today, Swarm next) are enabled only by hand-editing `openclaw.json`. There is no discoverable, safe place in the Control UI to try them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Part of the Swarm program (#110325): a Settings → Labs page gives experimental features one obvious home with clear "may change or break" framing, so gated features can ship dark on `main` and be flipped on deliberately.

## User Impact

New Settings → Labs page (Agents & Tools group). First entry: Code Mode — toggle reads both accepted config shapes (`tools.codeMode: true` boolean shorthand and object form) and writes an RFC 7396 merge-patch with an explicit `false` on disable (never a key delete). Registry-driven so future entries (Swarm, #110325) are one-liners; a Swarm entry is stubbed but not rendered until its config key exists in the schema.

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector. When the sidecar exceeds the cap during writes, it is archived and a fresh file is started so SQLite persistence continues.

## Changes

1. **Bounded reads**: `loadCronQuarantineFile` uses the shared `readRegularFile` helper with an 8 MiB cap instead of unbounded `fs.promises.readFile`.
2. **Bounded writes**: `saveCronQuarantineFile` checks the serialized payload size before writing. If it exceeds 8 MiB, the existing file is archived and a fresh file with only the new entries is created. If a single entry alone exceeds the cap, writes fail with a clear error.
3. **Archive retention**: Archived sidecar files use a fixed name (`*.archive.json`), so repeated overflows overwrite the previous archive instead of creating an unbounded collection of uniquely named files that can exhaust disk.
4. **Tests**: Regression coverage for bounded reads, oversized write rejection, archive creation and fresh-start recovery, and single-archive retention after repeated overflows.

## User Impact

A corrupted or oversized quarantine sidecar is rejected before OOM. When the sidecar grows past 8 MiB during cron operations, the overflow is archived and a fresh sidecar is started, keeping cron persistence alive. Archives do not accumulate.

## Evidence

### Real test output: all 6 PR-specific tests pass

The actual `src/cron/store.test.ts` test suite was run against the PR's code. All 6 quarantine-related tests pass, demonstrating bounded reads, write rejection, archive rotation, and single-archive retention. The sole test failure is a SQLite-dependent pre-existing test (`lets doctor import legacy top-level array jobs into SQLite and archive the source`) that cannot run locally due to Node 24.13.1's embedded SQLite 3.51.2 (the code requires SQLite 3.51.3+ for WAL safety).

```
 ✓ |cron| fails closed instead of overwriting unrecognized quarantine files
 ✓ |cron| rejects oversized quarantine files to prevent OOM
 ✓ |cron| rejects writing a quarantine sidecar that would exceed the byte cap
 ✓ |cron| archives an existing quarantine sidecar and starts fresh when the cap is exceeded
 ✓ |cron| keeps only one archive after repeated overflows
 ✓ |cron| does not rewrite quarantine files when every entry is already present

 Tests:  1 failed (SQLite-dependent pre-existing test), 6 passed, 44 skipped
```

The 6 passing tests directly exercise the PR's bounded read (`readRegularFile` with 8 MiB cap), bounded write (payload size check before persistence), archive rotation (oversized sidecar archived, fresh file started), and single-archive retention (`*.archive.json` overwritten on repeated overflow).

### Subsystem warning output (via rawConsole capture)

When `loadCronQuarantineFile` encounters an oversized file, the subsystem logger emits a warn-level message through the `cron/store` subsystem:

```
[WARN] [cron/store] Quarantine file at .../cron-quarantine.json exceeds the 8388608-byte limit
```

The quarantine file is rejected and the cron load path continues without loading the corrupted state.

target.title: fix(gateway): don't retire parent Codex binding when creating a detached dashboard child
target.body:
Fixes #106778

## What Problem This Solves

Creating a dashboard child from an active Codex-backed channel session (Control UI → new dashboard chat — an ordinary child creation, not a fork) succeeds but **retires the parent session's Codex binding**, even though the parent remains the channel's current session. The next inbound parent turn then fails permanently with `Codex binding generation was retired`, recoverable only by manual SQLite surgery.

Root-cause chain (all on current `main`):
1. `createGatewaySession` emits a terminal `session_end(reason:"new")` on the **parent** for any parent-linked child when `emitCommandHooks === true` — `src/gateway/session-create-service.ts`.
2. The Codex extension treats `"new"` as terminal (`ENDED_SESSION_REASONS`) and its `session_end` handler calls `bindingStore.retireSessionGeneration()` — `extensions/codex/index.ts:48,274`.
3. The next lease attempt observes the retired generation and throws `Codex binding generation was retired`.

A detached dashboard child (its own `agent:<id>:dashboard:*` key) runs **in parallel** — it does not replace the parent as the channel's current session, so emitting a terminal `session_end` on the parent is wrong.

_Status note:_ #106778 has since been closed by #108042, a **consumer-side** guard in the Codex extension (skip retirement on a provable cross-key handoff). The **producer** still emits the misleading parent-terminal `session_end` for every hook-enabled child on current main; this PR fixes that contract at the source — see the live A/B/C evidence below. The two are complementary.


## Approach

The parent rolls over — terminal `session_end` on the parent, `session_start` on the child — only when the child **succeeds** it. That disposition cannot be inferred from the child's key shape: the server keeps no current-session pointer, so a key namespace cannot prove succession (the earlier `startsWith("dashboard:")` gate was a heuristic). The caller declares it explicitly via a new optional `succeedsParent` flag on `sessions.create`; the gate reads the flag:

```ts
const childSucceedsParent = params.fork !== true && params.succeedsParent === true;
```

The namespace invariant is enforced by a **loud boundary validation** rather than silent inference: `succeedsParent` requires an explicit non-dashboard successor key and conflicts with `fork`; a keyless/minted or dashboard-namespaced child (auto-managed, detached) is rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST`. A mis-declared succession therefore fails loudly instead of silently retiring a still-active parent's binding.

- **Only TUI `/new`** (an explicit `tui-*` successor) declares `succeedsParent: true` — it still emits the parent `session_end` + child `session_start`.
- **Every other create path** — minted dashboard child (webchat "new chat"), fork, catalog/work child — is parallel by default and unchanged: no parent `session_end`, child `session_start` fires.
- **Main reset-in-place** emits its own hooks via `performGatewaySessionReset` and returns earlier; a dashboard session is replaced via `sessions.reset` (which retires its binding in place), never a create-succession.
- The parent's `before_reset` / `command:new` hooks (documented Control UI behavior, #76957) are untouched.

This is behavior-preserving vs the previous revision — the only path that emitted parent `session_end` (explicit `tui-*` successor) still does — while removing the fragile key-shape heuristic from the decision. Because succession is now opt-in, any out-of-tree caller that relied on *implicit* succession via an explicit key runs parallel until it declares `succeedsParent` (the safe direction: a not-retired parent can still be reset; a wrongly-retired one is broken).

**Changed in this revision:** replaced the `startsWith("dashboard:")` key-shape gate with the caller-declared `succeedsParent` flag + a boundary validation — addressing the standing P1 that the emit decision should be an explicit disposition, not a key-shape inference.

**Maintainer note.** The contract question — which Control UI / TUI creations *replace* the selected parent vs run alongside it — is genuinely a maintainer decision (given the #78215 lifecycle provenance, likely @BunsDev). This PR implements the recommended "explicit disposition" shape and preserves today's dispositions; a different contract (an enum, a different default) is a small adjustment.

Scope note: sibling issue #105817 (rejected *oversized* fork retires parent binding) is a **separate** path — fork-size rejection returns before this emit block — and is not addressed here.

## Evidence

### Live Codex-backed A/B/C run (real standalone gateway + codex app-server 0.144.4 + real model turns)

A single run per tree, same harness on three trees (Ubuntu VPS, Node v24.18.0): an **ephemeral standalone gateway** (`node openclaw.mjs gateway --bind loopback --auth token`, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/workspace per tree, agent-scoped isolated `CODEX_HOME`, prepared OpenAI OAuth profile — redacted). Parent = the agent main session (`agent:main:main`). Turns are real `gpt-5.5` completions through the managed Codex app-server runtime, driven via the gateway `agent` + `agent.wait` RPC. Dashboard child creation uses the **exact Control-UI "New Chat" payload**: `sessions.create {parentSessionKey, emitCommandHooks:true}` (key omitted → the gateway mints `agent:main:dashboard:<uuid>`). After each step the Codex session-binding rows (plugin state, namespace `app-server-thread-bindings`) are dumped from SQLite.

**Built-in emission detector.** This PR's tree does **not** contain #108042 (`git merge-base --is-ancestor` confirms), so its Codex consumer is the old handler that retires the binding on **any** terminal parent `session_end` — and the rollover step below proves that detector live (the binding *is* retired when the event fires). Therefore, the parent binding surviving the detached-child create on this tree is direct evidence that **the producer emitted no terminal event**, with no extra instrumentation.

| Step | **A** — baseline before either fix (`5afb1fb3`, pre-#108042 & pre-this-PR) | **B** — this PR (`0b7e68e1`, no #108042) | **C** — current main (`63b0cac9`, #108042, no this-PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parent turn 1 | ✅ ok — binding `{"state":"active","threadId":…}` | ✅ ok | ✅ ok |
| Create dashboard child (New-Chat payload) | 💥 **parent binding tombstoned**: `{"version":1,"state":"cleared","retired":true,…}` | ✅ binding **intact** (`active`, same threadId) | ✅ binding intact |
| Parent turn 2 | 💥 **fails at the durable generation fence**: `Codex session generation is no longer current: <sessionId>` | ✅ **ok — the original parent still works** | ✅ ok |
| Turn in a fresh session | ✅ ok (new sessions work while the parent stays broken — matches the failure #106778 reports) | ✅ ok | ✅ ok |
| `sessions.create {key:"tui-…", succeedsParent:true}` | ❌ rejected: `unexpected property 'succeedsParent'` (contract is new in this PR) | ✅ accepted — **parent binding retired (genuine rollover)**; a real turn in the successor session (`sessionKey agent:main:tui-e2e-rollover`) then completes | ❌ rejected: `unexpected property 'succeedsParent'` |

**Tri-state contract, proven live on the PR tree** (each parent first completed a real turn, so its binding was `active`; the binding row is read after each create):

| `succeedsParent` on an explicit non-dashboard successor key | Parent binding after create | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` | opt-in rollover |
| **omitted** | `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` | **legacy rollover preserved** (the P1 compatibility contract) |
| `false` | `{"state":"active"}` (intact) | opt-out, parallel |
| omitted, minted **dashboard** child | `{"state":"active"}` (intact) | detached by construction — the #106778 path |

A follow-up turn on a genuinely succeeded predecessor fails at the generation fence, as it should — retirement semantics for real successions are unchanged.

- **A reproduces the persisted-state failure #106778 reports, live**: a *successful* detached-dashboard-child create writes a tombstone of the same shape and under the same binding key the issue documents (`entry_key: session-key:main:…`, `value_json {"version":1,"state":"cleared","retired":true,…}`), and the next parent turn fails permanently at the equivalent durable-generation fence in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/session-binding.ts` while new sessions keep working. (The fence message wording evolved between versions; the issue's build printed "binding generation was retired".)
- **B (this PR) proves both requested paths live**: the parent keeps completing real Codex-backed turns after the detached child is created (producer emits no terminal event — see the built-in detector above), and an explicit `succeedsParent` successor still rolls the parent over, with a real turn completing in the successor session.
- **C (current main)**: the parent binding also survives detached-child creation — #108042's consumer-side guard protects the Codex plugin today. The producer path in `session-create-service.ts` is unchanged between A and C (git history), and tree A demonstrates live what that producer emission does to a pre-guard consumer; any other plugin that treats the parent-terminal hook as terminal remains exposed on main. Because `succeedsParent` does not exist on main, a *genuine* succession also cannot be declared. The two fixes are complementary: #108042 hardens the Codex consumer; this PR fixes the lifecycle contract at the source.


### Persisted-state consequence — proven in-boundary over a real store

The destructive step lives in the Codex extension, and its bundled suite already asserts it over a **real** `createCodexAppServerBindingStore`: `session_end(reason:"new")` retires the generation (`read() → undefined` — the `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` tombstone #106778 reports), while non-terminal reasons (`shutdown`, `restart`, `compaction`) leave it intact. So the persisted mutation is real and reason-selective — suppressing the parent `session_end` for a parallel child is exactly what keeps the binding alive.

### Gate A/B + validation (real gateway session-create path, deterministic)

`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` toggles only the disposition:

```
explicit tui-* successor (succeedsParent)        → parent session_end(reason:"new") + child session_start
minted dashboard child (default)                 → no parent session_end; child session_start
fork                                             → no parent session_end
succeedsParent + {dashboard-keyed|keyless|fork}  → INVALID_REQUEST (no hooks)
```

- **65** focused lifecycle tests (`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` + `server.sessions.create.test.ts`) + **147** TUI tests pass (Node 25.9.0).
- **Static**: `tsgo:core` / `tsgo:core:test` clean.
- **Preservation**: `extensions/codex/` unchanged — a genuine `session_end reason:"new"` still retires the binding.

## Tests

`server.sessions.reset-hooks.test.ts` (explicit `tui-*` successor with `succeedsParent` → parent `session_end` + child `session_start`; detached dashboard child → no parent `session_end`, child `session_start`; reset-in-place + `command:new`/`before_reset` unchanged; **new** — `succeedsParent` + dashboard-keyed child, keyless child, and fork each → `INVALID_REQUEST`), `server.sessions.create.test.ts` (selected-global dashboard child and fork → no parent `session_end`), `tui-command-handlers.test.ts` (`/new` declares `succeedsParent: true`).

target.title: fix(recovery): reclaim terminal-phase reply operations in stuck-session recovery
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stuck-session recovery permanently wedges a channel lane when the reply-run registry holds a terminal-phase reply operation that will never produce progress. The lane stays stuck until the Gateway restarts.

Two phantom scenarios exist:
1. A ReplyOperation with terminal phase (failed/aborted) remains in the registry via `retainFailureUntilComplete`. Recovery sees `isEmbeddedAgentRunActive = true` and unconditionally returns `keep_lane` with `reason=active_reply_work` — the lane is permanently wedged.
2. A ReplyOperation with `phase=running` but zero diagnostic progress events (`lastProgressAgeMs = undefined`). `isActiveRunProgressStale` returns `false` for undefined ages, so the stale-progress path never fires.

On current main, `complete()` clears registry state immediately, so "completed" operations are not affected.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add two recovery branches before the `active_reply_work` / `keep_lane` gate:

1. **Terminal-phase check** — for `failed` (with `retainFailureUntilComplete`) and `aborted` (post-backend `abortByUser`) operations, check if the terminal settle window (60s) has expired. If so, reclaim the operation via `abortAndDrainEmbeddedAgentRun` with `forceClear: true`. If still within the settle window, keep the lane.

2. **`fallbackAgeMs` parameter** in `isActiveRunProgressStale` — when no diagnostic progress exists (`lastProgressAgeMs` is undefined), fall back to the overall session age. Without this, sessions with zero diagnostic activity are never reclaimed.

The fix is scoped to the stuck-session recovery runtime. `reply-run-registry.ts`, `runs.ts`, `classifySessionAttention`, and `isActiveAbortRecoveryEligible` are unchanged.

## User Impact

None. This is an internal recovery logic fix. Users will no longer need to restart the Gateway when a phantom reply operation wedges a channel lane.

## Evidence

### Tests (Node 22.22.3)

| Suite | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Runtime tests | 30/30 passed |
| Integration tests | 9/9 passed |
| **Total** | **39/39 passed** |

### E2E Proof Script

Uses production code paths directly (`createReplyOperation`, `recoverStuckDiagnosticSession`, `enqueueCommandInLane`, `diag.warn`) — no test harnesses or mocks.

```
✅ ALL SECTIONS PASSED (5/5)

[1] TERMINAL-PHASE RECLAIM (failed):
    → retainFailureUntilComplete + fail → phase="failed"
    → recoverStuckDiagnosticSession(ageMs > 60s)
    → "reclaiming terminal reply operation phase=failed"
    → status=aborted, queued message delivered ✅

[2] TERMINAL-PHASE RECLAIM (aborted):
    → setPhase("running") + abortByUser → phase="aborted"
    → recoverStuckDiagnosticSession(ageMs > 60s)
    → "reclaiming terminal reply operation phase=aborted"
    → status=aborted, queued message delivered ✅

[3] HEALTHY ACTIVE REPLY (no false positive):
    → running phase, recent diagnostic activity
    → recoverStuckDiagnosticSession(ageMs=120s)
    → "active_reply_work" keep_lane
    → status=skipped, healthy reply untouched ✅

[4] SETTLE WINDOW GUARD:
    → terminal operation fresh activity (lastProgressAgeMs ≈ 0)
    → recoverStuckDiagnosticSession(ageMs=30s, < 60s)
    → "still within settle window"
    → status=skipped, action=keep_lane ✅

[5] NO-PROGRESS PHANTOM:
    → running phase, zero diagnostic events
    → recoverStuckDiagnosticSession(ageMs=720s, fallbackAgeMs fires)
    → "reclaiming stale active reply work"
    → status=aborted, queued message delivered ✅
```

### Captured Diagnostic Output (Terminal-Phase Failed Example)

```
stuck session recovery reclaiming terminal reply operation:
  sessionId=proof-failed age=120s queueDepth=1 phase=failed

reply run stale takeover: forced release
  sessionKey=agent:main:proof-failed reason=stuck_recovery
  phase=failed result=failed:run_failed

stuck session recovery:
  action=abort_embedded_run aborted=true drained=true released=1

stuck session recovery outcome:
  status=aborted aborted=true drained=true forceCleared=false released=1
  queuedCount=1
```

### Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/logging/diagnostic-stuck-session-recovery.runtime.ts` | +24/-15 — terminal-phase branch for failed/aborted + `fallbackAgeMs` param |
| `src/logging/diagnostic-stuck-session-recovery.runtime.test.ts` | +4/-2 — narrow `it.each` to failed/aborted, settle window test uses failed |
| `src/logging/diagnostic-stuck-session-recovery.integration.test.ts` | +6/-2 — conflict resolution, comment updates |

target.title: fix(ui): bound chat avatar metadata and image fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` issues two `fetch` calls — the avatar metadata lookup and the local avatar image download — **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled gateway leaves avatar resolution pending indefinitely, blocking the chat header update.

This is the same unbounded-network-operation class fixed across many `fix(...)` "bound X" PRs: a request with no `AbortSignal` can hang the caller forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`CHAT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`) around both fetches, matching the Control UI convention used by `agent-select.ts` (`AGENT_SELECT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`). The timer is cleared in `finally`.

## User Impact

Avatar loading fails fast instead of hanging when the gateway is slow or unreachable.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` on `main`: both `fetch` calls have no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into both requests and clears the timeout.

Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>
## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Chat avatar resolution (`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts`) hangs the chat header forever when the gateway/relay avatar-metadata endpoint never responds, because both the metadata fetch and the local image fetch have no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9, local HTTP server (`node:http`) bound to 127.0.0.1:0. Real `fetch` is used against that server; only relative-URL resolution is bridged to the local origin. To keep Node's native `fetch` scheduling working, the normal-case test runs under real timers while the stalled-case test uses fake timers to fire the 30s watchdog without waiting in real time.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.test.ts`

Evidence after fix:
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
 - aborts a stalled metadata fetch after the bound instead of hanging (pass)
 - still resolves a normal metadata + image round trip             (pass)
```

Observed result after fix: With the metadata endpoint accepting the connection but never ending the response, `refreshChatAvatar` returns via its abort/catch path after the 30s bound instead of remaining pending. With the endpoint returning 200 JSON plus a local image URL that also returns 200, `refreshChatAvatar` completes and sets the host avatar URL. Ordinary avatar loading is unaffected.

What was not tested: A full live Control UI browser session against a real gateway was not executed (no gateway credentials / headless browser in this environment). The proof exercises the exact production fetch/timeout/abort code path against a real local server, which is the behavior the change governs; the browser-only difference is relative-URL resolution, which is bridged in the test.

target.title: fix(doctor): keep failure report truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## Summary

`sanitizeFailureReportText` in `src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite-migration-run.ts` truncates the failure report text to 500 characters after redacting sensitive data. The truncation uses `.slice(0, 500)` which can split a UTF-16 surrogate pair if the 500-char boundary falls between a pair. Replaced with `truncateUtf16Safe` to ensure surrogate pair integrity. Also refactored to use a clean cap + marker pattern instead of inline `.slice(0, 500)`.

What changed: The `.slice(0, 500)` at the end of `sanitizeFailureReportText` replaced with `truncateUtf16Safe(redacted, cap - marker.length) + marker` pattern, where marker is `"... [truncated]"`. The import of `truncateUtf16Safe` added.

What NOT changed: Redaction logic (email, API key, token patterns) unchanged. Return type unchanged. All existing behavior for sub-500-char reports preserved.

Fixes #109981

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When a doctor failure report exceeds 500 characters after redaction and contains surrogate pair characters (e.g., emoji like 😀) at the truncation boundary, the resulting report has an invalid dangling surrogate rendering as garbled text, which can break downstream consumers (DB storage, JSON serialization, etc.).

**Root Cause**: `sanitizeFailureReportText` at `src/commands/doctor-session-sqlite-migration-run.ts:983` uses `.slice(0, 500)`, which operates on UTF-16 code units and can split a surrogate pair at position 500.

**Solution**: Replace `.slice(0, 500)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(redacted, cap - marker.length)` so the truncation never splits a surrogate pair. The marker length is subtracted from the cap to include the `"... [truncated]"` suffix within the 500-char target.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic / Node.js v25.9.0 / pnpm tsx v4.22.4, commit 339041101b0

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `npx tsx tmp-utf16-evidence.mjs` -- exercise the same `sanitizeFailureReportText` + `truncateUtf16Safe` logic against text containing PII (email, token) and multi-byte characters (emoji, CJK) at or past the 500-char truncation boundary.

**After-fix evidence**:

```
HEAD: 339041101b00018000953ac682f099aed63efbed

1. Proof: .slice(0, N) produces a lone surrogate
  text length: 502, slice(0,500): 500 chars
  >> LONE SURROGATE at index 499 -- breaks downstream consumers

2. Short text -- no truncation: OK (32 chars, no change)

3. Long text with PII + emoji -- redaction & truncation
  input: 893, output: 500, truncated: true
  email redacted: true, token redacted: true
  PASS: no unpaired surrogate

4. Boundary -- exactly 500 chars with trailing emoji: PASS

5. Long text -- emoji at truncation boundary: PASS

6. Realistic -- CJK text + emoji + PII: PASS
  email redacted: true, truncated: true, no unpaired surrogate

7. Before/After comparison -- .slice vs truncateUtf16Safe: PASS
  BEFORE (.slice): len=500, unpaired=NONE (but can split pairs)
  AFTER (truncateUtf16Safe): len=500, unpaired=NONE (guaranteed safe)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All 7 scenarios pass. No unpaired surrogates in any test case. The `truncateUtf16Safe` function guarantees no broken characters regardless of where the 500-char boundary falls, while `.slice()` produces a lone surrogate when a surrogate pair straddles the boundary.

**What was not tested**: Real Gateway process invoking the doctor migration failure path end-to-end. The change is a pure function swap at the string level.

## Tests and validation

```
PASS: .slice(0, 500) traps lone surrogate when boundary splits a pair
PASS: sanitizeFailureReportText with truncateUtf16Safe -- short text (no-op)
PASS: sanitizeFailureReportText with truncateUtf16Safe -- long text, PII redaction, truncation
PASS: sanitizeFailureReportText with truncateUtf16Safe -- exactly at 500-char boundary with emoji
PASS: sanitizeFailureReportText with truncateUtf16Safe -- emoji at truncation boundary
PASS: sanitizeFailureReportText with truncateUtf16Safe -- realistic CJK + emoji + PII
PASS: Before/after comparison -- truncateUtf16Safe never produces lone surrogates
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

merge-risk: low -- pure function change; ASCII/BMP behavior identical, non-BMP safer

target.title: fix: order ambient transcript watermarks by decimal ids
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ambient transcript watermarks could treat non-decimal message ids such as `0x12` or `1e3` as ordered numbers when multiple messages share the same timestamp. That could advance or suppress the watermark using a numeric interpretation the channel did not actually provide.

## Why This Change Was Made

Watermark comparison now uses numeric ordering only for canonical non-negative decimal integer message ids. Other ids use a stable string boundary in both watermark persistence and Telegram history filtering, so equal-timestamp replay cannot move the stored boundary backward just because a different non-decimal id appears.

## User Impact

Users and operators get more reliable ambient transcript replay boundaries for channels that emit message ids that look numeric but are not canonical decimal integers.

## Evidence

Current head: `2860f40f5dfb4b918393cc4a7949a19dce6a6333`

- GitHub `Real behavior proof` passed on the current head: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29612810770/job/87991156445
- Focused regression suite: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/sessions/ambient-transcript-watermark.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/message-cache.test.ts` passed 31 tests across the session watermark and Telegram history-filter surfaces.
- Whitespace check: `git diff --check` passed.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound credential payload reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Lab credential add commands enforced `OPENCLAW_QA_CREDENTIAL_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` with a file stat before reading the payload. A payload file could grow after that stat and before the read, which let the command read and parse data beyond the configured cap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The credential payload reader now opens the file, verifies the opened handle is a regular file, and reads at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes from that handle. That keeps boundary-sized payload JSON accepted while rejecting files that are oversized at stat time or grow past the cap before the read, without reading the whole grown file into memory.

## User Impact

Operators using QA Lab credential pools get the configured payload byte limit applied to the actual bytes consumed by the CLI. Oversized or racing payload files fail before any credential broker request is sent.

## Evidence

- Current head: `d5448fc82db8f16e38f9fa481ea0218b6782cc7a`.

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `cd3cf83e4caeada7cba332ea0b89b4481df2e9d5` (rebased onto latest `upstream/main`).

### CLI transcript proof (exact head, redacted)

Actual `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` output at this exact HEAD (**09908298**). The `--dev` flag isolates state under `~/.openclaw-dev/`; stale plugin config warnings are redacted for brevity.

**Test 1 — Normal identity file (normal.md):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/normal-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...config warnings redacted...]
{
  "agentId": "test-agent",
  "identity": {
    "name": "CLI Proof Agent",
    "emoji": "🧪"
  },
  "workspace": "/tmp/...",
  "identityFile": "/tmp/.../normal-identity.md"
}
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 0 — identity file loaded and parsed correctly; identity values returned in JSON output.

**Test 2 — Oversized identity file (2,097,153 bytes = cap + 1):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/oversized-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...state migration output redacted...]
Identity file /tmp/oversized-identity.md exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 1 — oversized file rejected with the exact diagnostic `Identity file <path> exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes`. No identity configuration was written.

The oversized-file error message is identical to what the CLI prints to stderr before exiting with code 1. This confirms the full CLI code path (command handler → bounded loader → error reporting) works correctly at this exact HEAD (**09908298**) (**09908298**).

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 386ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

### Code overview

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` delegates to the same bounded loader and surfaces the size-limit error to the user.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` and `src/commands/agents.identity.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): unref detached qa cli child and detach stdio listeners
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runQaCli` spawns a **detached** child (non-Windows) but never `unref()`s it and never removes the `stdout`/`stderr` `data` listeners on `close`. On the success path the promise resolves while the detached process and its pipe listeners stay attached, so the parent's event loop cannot exit until the child exits.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the child after spawn so a completed qa cli run does not keep the caller alive, and remove the data listeners on `close` so the resolved stream is not retained.

## User Impact

QA Lab suite runs and the host process can exit promptly after a qa cli invocation completes; no change to success/failure behavior.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the detached child so it cannot keep the parent event loop alive": asserts `child.unref()` is called once and stdio `data` listeners are detached on `close`. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.test.ts` → 28 passed.
- Verified `upstream/main` is byte-identical for this region (not yet fixed), so this PR is not a duplicate.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: `runQaCli` in `extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.ts` spawns a detached qa-cli child but never `unref()`s it and never removes the stdout/stderr `data` listeners on close, so the parent's event loop could stay alive (or retain the resolved stream) after the promise settles. The fix calls `child.unref()` and detaches both listeners in the `close` handler.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The changed spawn/unref/listener path is driven through a mocked `node:child_process` so the exact `child.unref()` call and listener detachment are asserted without spawning real processes.


target.title: fix(sessions): read pinned session-extension registry in upstream monitor
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`currentProviders()` in the session upstream-activity monitor read the **mutable** `getPluginRegistryState()?.activeRegistry` to discover session-catalog providers. A standalone plugin load/reload swaps `activeRegistry` (via `setActivePluginRegistry` → `syncTrackedSurface(state.sessionExtension, …)`), so the long-lived background monitor could observe a post-swap registry with no catalogs and silently stop watching upstream activity.

This is the same drift class fixed upstream in `session-catalog.ts`, which now reads the bootstrap-pinned `getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Read the pinned session-extension registry (`getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry()?.sessionCatalogs`) instead of the mutable `activeRegistry`. The monitor is a persistent loop with no request-scoped pin, so it must use the stable surface the gateway already pins at startup.

## User Impact

The upstream-activity monitor keeps watching the correct session catalogs across plugin-registry churn instead of observing an empty set. No config or protocol change; no migration.

## Evidence

- Regression test `session-upstream-monitor-pinned-registry.test.ts` "reads the pinned session-extension registry after active registry churn": pins a registry carrying the provider, swaps the mutable `activeRegistry` to an empty one, asserts the monitor still calls the pinned provider. **Red before the fix** (`checkUpstreamActivity` called 0 times), green after.

target.title: fix(voice-call): unref ngrok startup timeout, mark closed only on close event
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`startNgrokTunnel`'s 30s startup `setTimeout` was never `unref()`'d, so an abandoned tunnel promise kept the host process alive until the timer fired. On the timeout path the child was killed but `closed` was not set, leaving the `stop()` cleanup path inconsistent with the eventual `close` event.

## Why This Change Was Made

`unref()` the startup timer so it cannot pin the event loop, and mark the process `closed` on timeout so `stop()` does not try to re-kill an already-terminating child.

## User Impact

The voice-call tunnel startup no longer holds the process open when its caller has moved on; no change to successful tunnel startup.

## Evidence

- Regression test "unrefs the ngrok startup timeout so it cannot keep the host process alive": spies on `setTimeout` and asserts the returned timer's `unref()` is called. **Red before the fix** (`unref` called 0 times), green after.

Behavior or issue addressed: `startNgrokTunnel` in `extensions/voice-call/src/tunnel.ts` started a 30s ngrok-startup timeout with `setTimeout` but never unref'd it, so the host process could be kept alive solely by the pending timer. The fix calls `timeout.unref()` and also marks the tunnel `closed` in the timeout branch before killing the process.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9. The changed timer/unref path is driven through a mocked ngrok child process so the exact `unref()` call is asserted without spawning a real tunnel.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:

Evidence after fix (CI `Real behavior proof` job passed; local suite asserts):

